beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson six. The electron transport chain. [[mill]]A water wheel turns because water falls. If it dropped all at once, from the top of a cliff, the wheel would be smashed. A staircase of small drops lets the energy be used. [[map]]Here is our map of cellular respiration again. [[lit]]Glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle have done their work. Now we light the last stage, oxidative phosphorylation, and its first part, the electron transport chain.
beats.carriers: [[carriers]]After glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, most of the energy that came out of the glucose is carried by two molecules: N A D H and F A D H two. They are loaded with electrons, and they donate them to the electron transport chain. [[where]]The chain sits in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion, the membrane folded into cristae. [[folds]]Those folds give the membrane much more surface, so there is room for a great many chains. [[parts]]Most of the parts of the chain are proteins, grouped into multiprotein complexes. We number them one, two, three and four.
beats.chain: [[nadh]]N A D H meets complex one first. Its two electrons drop into the complex, and the empty N A D plus is released, free to go back and be loaded again. [[fadh]]F A D H two joins lower down, at complex two. Same kind of pass, but it starts from a lower step. [[q]]Both hand their electrons to a small carrier called ubiquinone, or Q, which is not a big protein complex. It moves within the membrane, and carries the electrons on to complex three. [[cytc]]From there a small protein, cytochrome c, takes them to complex four. Cytochromes are proteins with an iron atom, and that iron is what holds the electrons for a moment. [[redox]]Every carrier along the way takes electrons and becomes reduced, then passes them on and becomes oxidized again. Reduced, oxidized, reduced, oxidized, all the way down.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where does N A D H hand over its electrons?
beats.stairs: [[axis]]Now let's see the energy. This graph shows free energy, going up, in kilocalories per mole. The electrons from N A D H start near the top, at about fifty. [[down]]Each carrier sits a little lower than the one before, so the electrons fall in free energy, step by step. [[fadh2]]Electrons from F A D H two enter lower, at about forty three. They have less distance left to fall, so F A D H two gives the cell less than N A D H does. [[end]]At the bottom, the electrons are at about ten, and there is one last step to oxygen.
beats.oxygen: [[o2]]The final acceptor is oxygen. [[water]]Oxygen takes the two electrons, picks up two protons, and with half an oxygen molecule makes water. This is the water that cellular respiration gives off. [[pull]]And notice what oxygen does. It pulls electrons down the whole chain, because it is so electronegative. If oxygen is missing, the electrons have nowhere to go, and the chain backs up and stops. That is why we breathe.
beats.q2: Quick check. Does the chain itself make A T P?
beats.steps: [[no]]Here is a surprising fact. The electron transport chain makes no A T P itself. [[break]]Its job is to break the large free energy drop, from food to oxygen, into smaller steps. [[small]]Each step releases energy in a manageable amount, instead of one blast. [[later]]What the cell does with that energy, building a gradient of protons and using it to make A T P, is the story of lesson seven.
beats.example: Let's try numbers. [[sum]]Starting from about fifty kilocalories per mole, the electrons from N A D H fall to zero at oxygen. That is a drop of about fifty. [[split]]Spread over the complexes, each step releases only a fraction of that. [[fad]]Electrons from F A D H two start near forty three, so their total fall is about seven less. [[note]]These values are read off the slide's graph, so treat them as approximate. Textbooks give a little more for N A D H, around fifty two.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]N A D H and F A D H two carry the electrons to the chain, which sits in the cristae of the inner membrane. [[s2]]Electrons pass through complexes one to four, Q and cytochromes, falling in free energy, until oxygen takes them and forms water. [[s3]]The chain makes no A T P itself. It cuts one big drop into small steps. [[end]]Now try the practice.
